title: Pulling Out Teeth Just to Live: How Israel Has Devastated Dental Care in Gaza
author: Mohanad El-Hemrawi

DEIR AL-BALAH, Gaza Strip--At midnight, inside a tent in Deir al-Balah, Nour
Abo Shamala put her head against the pillow with a plastic cup of salt water
beside her. Sleep didn't come. A bolt of pain ran from her front tooth to the
top of her skull and across her head. The only sounds in the night were the
wind outside and her groans. She felt around for the plastic cup in the
darkness and rinsed her mouth with the water. It brought no relief to the ache
in her upper jaw. She soaked a rag in cold water, pressed it against her
mouth, and waited for dawn.

Abo Shamala, 22, has lived with this chronic pain since February. She
graduated university with a teaching degree just before the genocide began in
October 2023, and has never had the chance to work. The family lives on aid.
They were displaced from their home in Jabaliya more than five times before
reaching Deir al-Balah in May 2024.

This past May, three months after the pain in her tooth first began, she went
to one of the few dentists still working in the area. The decay had reached
the nerve, the dentist told her, and the tooth needed root canal treatment, or
she would lose it. It would cost 300 shekels (about $100). She told him she
couldn't afford to pay it. The dentist said the only other option was to
remove the tooth for 50 shekels (about $16).

"I can't pay 300 shekels, and if I have them, it would go to things that
matter more," Abo Shamala told Drop Site News. "I'm a girl. Imagine me without
a front tooth. How would I laugh or talk to people?" She also knew she
wouldn't be able to have the pulled tooth replaced any time soon. The dentist
warned her that the infection would worsen, and that the tooth was eroding
from the inside and could break at any moment.

The waiting has cost her. Months of painkillers left her with an inflamed
stomach, diagnosed at a UNRWA clinic. She can no longer bite into bread or
fruit, and cuts her food into small pieces to chew on her back teeth. "If the
treatment was 80 shekels the way it used to be, I wouldn't have waited a
single day," Abo Shamala said. Seven months on, her tooth is still salvageable
but she is still waiting for the price for root canal treatment to come down.

Over the past three years, proper dental care in Gaza has been all but
destroyed, along with the rest of the enclave's health care system, devastated
by sustained targeted attacks by the Israeli military and a crippling siege
that includes vital medical supplies.

Israeli airstrikes have destroyed 80 percent of the dental clinics in Gaza,
completely or partially, and more than 100 dentists have been killed since the
genocide began, according to Irfan Eshtaiwi, the head of the dentists'
syndicate in Gaza's southern governorates. The syndicate receives daily
notices from dentists who are shutting down or scaling back to emergency care
only. Beyond the blocked supplies, the clinics that remain are working without
reliable electricity, running water, or sterilization materials.

Another patient with dental issues faced the same difficult choice as Abo
Shamala but made a different decision.

Ahmed Abo Dan, 34, sells chocolate from a small street stand in Deir-al-Balah.
He was displaced from his home in northern Gaza in October 2023, after the
Israeli military issued sweeping displacement orders for the 1.1 million
Palestinians living north of Wadi Gaza to move to the south. In March, Abo Dan
began suffering from pain in his tooth. Painkillers were largely unavailable
at the local government clinic, and he often could not afford to buy them
himself, forcing him to endure the constant ache.

When he finally saw a dentist in June 2026, he was given two options for his
molar: a root canal treatment for 450 shekels (around $145), or extraction for
30 shekels (around $10). "I'm displaced and can barely scrape together the
price of a bag of bread for my children," Abo Dan told Drop Site. He chose
extraction, and borrowed the 30 shekels from a friend to pay for the
procedure. The tooth was pulled in July.

"War has made us pull out our teeth just to live," he said. Another tooth has
started to hurt him. "I'm afraid to go and be told I need treatment I can't
pay for all over again and maybe lose another tooth."

Hardly any dental supplies have entered Gaza since October 2023, according to
both Eshtaiwi and Dr. Osama Jaber Al-Shanti, the former dean of the Faculty of
Dentistry at the University of Palestine. Last month, Al-Shanti took part in a
demonstration by dozens of dentists who gathered in their white coats outside
the headquarters of the International Committee of the Red Cross in western
Gaza City to demand the entry of dental supplies into Gaza. The siege has
continued in violation of a "ceasefire" that went into effect over a year ago.

"They claim these are dual-use materials," Al-Shanti told Drop Site. "It's a
label used to evade and restrict, to keep useful materials out of Gaza." Small
quantities do get in, he said, through a limited number of private traders who
pay very high fees to bring them through, and those black market costs are
then built into the price of services offered by clinics.

Before the genocide, a syringe of resin used for fillings that cost 70 to 80
shekels (around $23-26), now costs 1,200 shekels (around $388), according to
Al-Shanti, an increase of 1,500%. Root canal treatment, which cost 70 to 150
shekels before the genocide, now runs 500 to 700 shekels at most clinics, Al-
Shanti said. He charges 300, because he is still working through inventory he
purchased earlier at a lower price and in bulk. The 300 does not cover his
costs, yet he maintains the price to avoid turning away patients.

At Al-Shanti's clinic in the Rimal neighborhood of Gaza City earlier this
month, three people sat waiting--a mother with her young son and a man resting
his cheek in his hand. It's the third clinic Al-Shanti has had to set up from
scratch since October 2023, after Israel destroyed two of his previous clinics
in strikes and displacement forced him to abandon another.

The clinic has none of the sharp anesthetic smell that usually permeates
dental offices. In the treatment room, a scratched yellow chair with a rusted
base stood against freshly painted walls, fitted with a new control board and
basin. The chair is the only piece of equipment that survived his second
clinic, bombed in early 2024. He pulled it from the rubble with a ruined
control board and a broken basin. A technician managed to repair the chair by
fitting parts from a chair destroyed in another Israeli strike. The repairs
cost Al-Shanti more than a new unit would have with spare parts also
skyrocketing in price, but he had no choice with no new dental equipment being
allowed into Gaza.

At his clinic, Al-Shanti is still able to provide fillings, extractions and
root canals. However he has been forced to stop implants, whitening, bridges,
and dentures due to a lack of supplies. He said his was one of the few dental
clinics still operational. Most of his colleagues have stopped working
altogether.

Ayman al-Shabrawi, who owns a dental laboratory in the Al-Saha area of Gaza
City, told Drop Site he has closed part of it and laid off two thirds of his
staff, and expects to shut the rest if medical supplies continue to be
blocked.

The Gaza Center for Human Rights said in August that Israel bars a wide range
of purely therapeutic dental materials and equipment under the dual-use label,
and that the resulting prices have pushed dentists toward tooth extraction as
the only remaining option. In Khan Younis governorate, the center said, only
one government dental clinic and two UNRWA clinics are still operating,
alongside a small number of private practices.

In March 2025, Al-Shanti screened children in displacement camps in Deir al-
Balah and Khan Younis for a Save the Children Netherlands program, which also
carried out medical screening for orphans. He found large numbers of children
with untreated decay that no one was following up on, and whose families could
not take them to a dentist. Malnutrition, he said, has made it worse. Most of
the children in Gaza are not examined at all, he said.

Warda Shaath, a dentist in Khan Yunis, said most dental treatment has to be
rationed because supplies are simply not available. Light-cured fillings, for
example, have disappeared from the market, she said. Some procedures that cost
around 50 shekels (around $16) before the genocide now cost close to 250
shekels (around $81).

About 90 percent of her patients now ask to have the tooth pulled rather than
to receive treatment, she said, because they cannot pay for a filling or a
root canal. If the supply shortage continues, she is considering closing down
the clinic next month.

Shaath still does implants, with materials she buys on the black market at
very high prices. One of her patients, a 32-year-old mother of four, lost
several teeth when her house collapsed on her. She needs four implants. The
full treatment would cost around 10,000 shekels (around $3,300), and the first
stage alone would cost close to 5,000 shekels (around $1,615). Shaath said the
clinic tried to find a way to cover the costs but they were unable to, and the
woman left in tears.

Dentists say they want to help their patients but are left without any options
with the ongoing Israeli siege.

"The moment supplies enter, the first thing I will do is message all my
patients and drop my prices immediately," Al-Shanti said. The profession has a
human side, he said, and is not only about profit.

Back in her tent, Nour Abo Shamala's front tooth is growing weaker and darker.
A small piece broke off the edge of the tooth recently when she bit down on a
piece of dry bread. She is still waiting for Israel to allow supplies to come
in, so the prices can come down.
